title: How to Fire People
author: Karol Wójciszko
summary: Karol Wójciszko, an engineering leader, shares his playbook for firing people, built from letting people go for performance, economic and collaboration reasons. He argues that managers improvise one of the hardest conversations in management and that improvisation is where it goes wrong, through small talk, passive language and unwanted consoling. The playbook starts from the rule that nobody should be surprised, so that a firing is a consequence and not a punishment. The meeting itself follows five steps: open with the decision in the first person, give the reason in a sentence or two, let the person react without consoling or debating, cover the logistics, then take questions and close. He insists it is not a negotiation and that the sentence ending the contract must start with "I". After the meeting he sends a written summary, notifies HR, and tells the team in circles, closest team first, without turning the topic into a taboo. Note that some scripted examples in the original post are limited to paid subscribers.
points: A firing should be a consequence the person could have foreseen; if the reason would not be recognized in one sentence, the feedback conversation was skipped.
State the decision in the first person within the first ten seconds, with no small talk, and avoid "the company decided" because it pushes responsibility elsewhere.
After the news, give a moment of silence and do not debate, defend fairness or console, then move to concise logistics.
Book 30 minutes and expect 15, and schedule emotional conversations at the end of the day or on a Friday afternoon so the person has time to absorb it.
Send a written summary straight after, tell the closest team first and name the general category of the reason, and treat the departure as a normal professional fact.
quotes: If someone is surprised they’re being fired, you failed long before the meeting.
A firing should be a consequence. The person knew what was expected, heard several times that it wasn’t happening, and had a real chance to change it.
The decision goes first, in the first person, within the first ten seconds. You don’t make them guess where this is going.
Whatever the reaction, don’t respond to the emotion and don’t start consoling.
First, this is not a negotiation. The decision has been made. You’re not there to discuss it, reconsider it or find a middle ground.
The passive voice feels safer, but it pushes the responsibility somewhere else. The person hears that you don’t stand behind it.
So I send a summary email right after the meeting. Dates, handover, next steps, contacts. Everything in writing.
Your team should hear that you ended the collaboration with someone, not hear from that person that they got fired.
Managers delay the decision because they’re afraid of the confrontation. Meanwhile the person keeps struggling, the team keeps compensating, and the manager keeps carrying it around.
